title: AI Recovery Is the New Cyber Resilience Gap
summary: Recovering from an attack like this means proving the business can safely resume operations, not just restoring a backup.
body_markdown:
#### Key Takeaways


- As AI becomes embedded in critical business processes, resilience must become part of the deployment conversation.


- Recovering AI is about more than restoring infrastructure. It’s about restoring confidence in the systems, data, and outputs that drive business decisions.


- Many organizations are moving AI into production faster than they are preparing to recover it when disruption occurs.


- Traditional disaster recovery plans provide a strong foundation, but they were not designed to address the unique challenges of AI.


- Organizations that prioritize AI resilience today will be better positioned to maintain trust, continuity, and business performance tomorrow.


Your organization probably knows how to recover a server, an application, or a database. Years of investment in cyber resilience have made disaster recovery a standard part of operating a business.


But what about an AI system?


As AI becomes embedded in business operations, a new resilience challenge is emerging. Organizations have moved quickly to deploy AI, but few have considered how they would recover models, datasets, vector databases, agents, and AI-driven workflows after a disruption.


New research from Sentinel Nexus examines how prepared organizations are to recover the AI systems they increasingly rely on. The report,


From AI Adoption to AI Recovery: Staying Clean and Provable,


is based on responses from 107 CISOs and senior security leaders. The findings highlight a concerning gap:


- 82% of organizations have deployed AI beyond piloting.


- Only 9% have updated resilience frameworks for AI-specific failure modes.


- Only 10% have tested AI recovery from a verified clean backup.


These numbers expose what may be one of the most important resilience challenges organizations face over the next several years: AI adoption is advancing faster than AI recovery readiness.


#### AI Has Become Production Infrastructure


One of the clearest findings from the research is that AI is no longer confined to experiments and innovation teams. Organizations are using AI to improve employee productivity, support customer engagement, automate workflows, and augment decision-making. In many cases, AI is already part of the operational backbone of the business.


Once a technology becomes critical to how a business operates, recovering it becomes a business concern, not just an IT concern. Organizations have long invested in protecting the systems that keep the business running because they understand the cost of downtime.


As AI becomes embedded in critical processes, it deserves the same level of attention. Yet many organizations still govern AI as an emerging technology initiative, even as it becomes an operational dependency.


#### Why AI Breaks Traditional Recovery Assumptions


Traditional recovery planning was built around restoring applications and infrastructure. If a system went down, the goal was to bring it back online and return to normal operations.


AI systems are more complicated.


An AI application may depend on models, training data, vector databases, prompts, orchestration layers, retrieval systems, and autonomous agents. Recovering infrastructure alone doesn’t necessarily restore the full system.


AI failures also can be harder to spot. A service outage is obvious, but an AI system may continue operating while generating inaccurate or unreliable outputs. Recovery isn’t just about restoring availability. It’s about restoring trust.


That changes the question from


*“Can we restore it?”* to


*“Can we trust what we’ve restored?”*


The report found that concerns about corrupted AI data and verifying recovered AI systems rank among organizations’ top recovery risks. Ultimately, confidence in recovery will matter as much as recovery itself.


#### The Gap Between Adoption and Resilience


Every technology transformation creates a period where adoption outpaces governance, and AI resilience is following the same pattern.


The significance of the gap – where 82% have deployed AI, but only 9% have frameworks for AI failures – goes beyond preparedness. It suggests that many organizations have reached a point where AI is influencing business outcomes, customer experiences, and day-to-day operations faster than resilience strategies can adapt.


Given how quickly AI has moved into production, that’s not surprising. Most resilience programs were built for applications, infrastructure, and data. AI introduces new dependencies, new recovery requirements, and new questions around trust, integrity, and validation that many organizations are only beginning to address.


As AI becomes a permanent part of how work gets done, resilience can no longer be treated as a follow-on activity. The organizations that mature their recovery capabilities alongside their AI investments will be better positioned to manage disruption, maintain trust, and realize long-term value from AI.


#### Why Existing Disaster Recovery Plans Aren’t Enough


Many organizations assume their existing disaster recovery capabilities will naturally extend to AI systems. The reality is more complicated.


More than half of respondents recognize a gap between their traditional recovery procedures and their ability to recover AI-specific systems. Given the speed of AI adoption, that’s not entirely unexpected. Most recovery programs were built to protect applications, infrastructure, and data. AI introduces a new set of dependencies that many organizations are only beginning to account for.


The gap becomes most visible during recovery testing. Organizations routinely validate their ability to recover critical applications and infrastructure, but AI is often left out of those exercises. As a result, many leaders have limited visibility into whether their existing recovery processes would work for AI systems.


Organizations can’t assume AI recovery will work simply because traditional IT recovery does. Recovery readiness has to be tested, validated, and demonstrated.


#### What Organizations Should Do Next


Closing the resilience gap doesn’t require organizations to slow down AI adoption. It requires treating AI as a recoverable business system and asking a different set of questions.


Which AI systems are truly business-critical? Who owns their resilience? What needs to be protected, recovered, and validated if those systems fail?


It also requires a broader view of what needs to be recovered. AI resilience extends beyond infrastructure to include models, datasets, vector stores, agent workflows, prompts, and the other assets that shape AI outcomes.


Ultimately, AI recovery isn’t just about getting systems back online. It’s about enabling the business to continue operating when disruption occurs.


The findings from the Sentinel Nexus report suggest many organizations are still early in their AI recovery journey. But as AI becomes more deeply embedded in business operations, the ability to recover it will become just as important as the ability to rely on it.

#### FAQs


**Q: What is AI recovery?**
**A:** AI recovery is the ability to restore AI systems and associated assets, including models, datasets, vector databases, prompts, agents, and workflows, after a disruption, cyberattack, or operational failure.


**Q: Why is AI recovery different from traditional disaster recovery?**
**A:** AI recovery is different from traditional disaster recovery because organizations must restore not only infrastructure and applications, but also the models, data sources, and workflows that influence AI outcomes. A recovered AI system may remain operational while still producing inaccurate, compromised, or untrustworthy results.


**Q: What is the AI resilience gap?**
**A:** The AI resilience gap is the growing disconnect between how quickly organizations are adopting AI and how prepared they are to recover AI systems after a disruption. Many organizations have operationalized AI, but few have updated resilience strategies or tested AI recovery procedures.


**Q: What is clean AI recovery?**
**A:** Clean AI recovery is the process of restoring AI systems and verifying that models, datasets, vector databases, and workflows are accurate, trusted, and free from corruption or compromise before returning them to production.


**Q: Why is AI resilience important?**
**A:** AI resilience is important because AI systems are increasingly supporting business-critical operations, customer experiences, and decision-making processes. Organizations need the ability to recover AI systems quickly while maintaining confidence in the accuracy and integrity of their outputs.


**Q: Where should organizations start with AI resilience?**
**A:** Organizations should start by identifying business-critical AI systems, assigning ownership for AI resilience, expanding recovery planning to include AI assets, and regularly testing AI recovery procedures to validate readiness.


**Q: What should be included in an AI recovery strategy?**
**A:** An AI recovery strategy should include protection and recovery plans for models, datasets, vector databases, prompts, configurations, agent workflows, supporting infrastructure, and the processes used to verify the integrity of recovered AI systems.


**Q: How can organizations validate a recovered AI system?**
**A:** Organizations can validate a recovered AI system by confirming the integrity of its models, datasets, workflows, and supporting assets, and by testing that the system produces expected outputs after recovery.
